Task and constraints: Count triples of positive side lengths that satisfy the strict triangle inequality.
Idea: Sort nums, fix the largest side nums[i], and use two pointers to count pairs among earlier values whose sum exceeds it.
Technique and why it applies: If nums[left]+nums[right] is greater than nums[i], then every value between left and right also works with right, so right-left triples are counted at once. Otherwise left advances.
Invariant: The sorted prefix before i is searched for pairs whose sum exceeds the fixed largest side.
Edge cases: Zero sides are naturally excluded by the inequality. Sorting mutates nums.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n) and the nested two-pointer scan is O(n²), with O(1) extra space beyond sorting. The author labels are conventional.

Task and constraints: Schedule tasks with a cooldown n between identical task types, minimizing total intervals.
Idea: Use a max-heap of remaining task counts and a queue holding tasks that are cooling down until a future timer value.
Technique and why it applies: Each time unit executes the most frequent available task. A decremented count is placed in the queue with its next available time; once the timer reaches that time, it returns to the heap.
Invariant: The heap contains currently available task counts and the queue contains unfinished tasks not yet eligible for reuse.
Edge cases: Idle intervals are represented by timer increments when the heap is empty. deque, defaultdict, and heappush are used without imports in the shown snippet.
Complexity: Heap and queue operations cost O(T log U) for T task executions and U task types, while the queue uses O(U·n) in the worst case. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum product obtainable from any three numbers in nums, including negative values.
Idea: Sort nums descending and compare the three largest values against the largest value multiplied by the two smallest values.
Technique and why it applies: The best product is either three largest positives or one large positive with two negative values whose product is positive. Sorting makes both candidate products directly available at the ends.
Invariant: nums[0:3] are the three largest values, and nums[-2:] are the two smallest values after descending sort.
Edge cases: The array must contain at least three values. Sorting mutates nums; the comments' claim of O(1) extra space depends on the sorting implementation.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), and selecting the two candidate products is O(1). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum product of any three values in the array.
Idea: Track the three largest values and two smallest values in one pass.
Technique and why it applies: The maximum product comes from either the three largest values or the largest value times the two smallest values, which may both be negative. The running minima/maxima are updated as each number is read.
Invariant: min1/min2 are the two smallest seen values and max1/max2/max3 are the three largest seen values, with duplicates allowed.
Edge cases: At least three numbers are assumed. The comparisons use <= and >= so repeated values can occupy multiple tracked positions.
Complexity: Each element updates a fixed number of variables, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, matching the author labels.

Task and constraints: Count permutations of length n having exactly k inverse pairs, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Use a one-dimensional DP and a sliding prefix sum to compute the number of permutations with each inversion count.
Technique and why it applies: Adding the next largest value can introduce between zero and i inversions. The running sum includes previous DP values in that range and subtracts the value that falls outside the window.
Invariant: dp[j] counts permutations of the previous size with j inverse pairs; tmp[j] builds the count for the next size.
Edge cases: k=0 has one increasing permutation. The loop iterates i from zero through n-1, which is the expected count of adding elements; indentation in comments is irregular but not executable.
Complexity: The loops take O(nk) time and O(k) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Count permutations of size n with exactly k inverse pairs.
Idea: Apply the sliding-window DP recurrence using a fresh array for each permutation size.
Technique and why it applies: The number of ways for j inversions is the previous count plus the preceding prefix count, minus the count that would add too many inversions when the new value is inserted.
Invariant: dp[j] stores the count for the current permutation size, and new_dp[j] is computed for the next size.
Edge cases: dp[0] begins at one for the empty permutation. Negative modular results are normalized by Python's modulo operator.
Complexity: The n-by-(k+1) loops take O(nk) time and two arrays use O(k) space, matching the author labels.

Task and constraints: Compute the number of permutations with exactly k inverse pairs, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Maintain a running prefix sum curr while filling the next DP row, subtracting the term that leaves the valid insertion window.
Technique and why it applies: The recurrence sums previous counts for a range of inversion totals. A sliding window avoids recomputing each sum from scratch and keeps each state update constant time.
Invariant: curr is the modular sum of the previous-row DP values allowed for the current j.
Edge cases: The initial dp[0]=1 represents the empty permutation. The subtraction occurs when j-(i+1) is nonnegative, removing values outside the window.
Complexity: Each of n rows computes k+1 entries, giving O(nk) time and O(k) space. The author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Count permutations with exactly k inverse pairs.
Idea: Explicitly construct candidate permutations for each inversion count by inserting the next value at different positions.
Technique and why it applies: Each insertion position changes the inversion count by a predictable amount; the nested comprehensions build all candidates corresponding to each DP bucket. The final assertion attempts to verify the count of inverse pairs.
Invariant: dp[j] is intended to hold all permutations with j inverse pairs after the current value has been inserted.
Edge cases: This approach materializes permutation lists and grows combinatorially. The assertion's sum expression and comparison should be checked carefully; it may not validate each candidate as intended.
Complexity: Runtime and storage are exponential in n because the code explicitly enumerates permutations, unlike a count-only DP. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Count permutations of size n with exactly k inverse pairs.
Idea: Build lists of permutations by inserting each new value into positions that produce each inversion count.
Technique and why it applies: For each current permutation p and insertion offset, the code inserts i into a position intended to add the corresponding number of inversions. The final bucket length is returned modulo MOD.
Invariant: dp[j] is intended to contain every generated permutation with j inverse pairs after processing the current values.
Edge cases: The list-based construction can consume enormous memory even for modest n. The assertion sums pair comparisons in a way that should be validated against the intended inverse-pair count.
Complexity: Explicit permutation enumeration has factorial-scale time and memory in the worst case. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Count permutations with exactly k inverse pairs, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Recompute each DP state by summing all valid previous inversion counts with reduce.
Technique and why it applies: Inserting a new largest element can create from zero through i inversions, so each dp[j] sums a range of earlier states. The reduce expression implements this sum directly instead of using a sliding-window recurrence.
Invariant: dp[j] stores the number of permutations of the current size with j inverse pairs.
Edge cases: dp[0] starts at one. The list comprehension rebinds dp only after the full row is built, so each row reads the prior row consistently.
Complexity: Each of n rows computes k states and each state sums O(n) terms, giving O(n²k) time and O(k) space. The author labels match this slow implementation.

Task and constraints: Count permutations of length n with exactly k inverse pairs.
Idea: Use a sliding-window dynamic program, trimming each row to the maximum possible inversion count for that size.
Technique and why it applies: The recurrence adds the previous row's count and the preceding prefix total, then subtracts the value falling outside the allowed inversion window. new_dp's length grows only as far as the current size permits, capped at k+1.
Invariant: dp contains counts for the previous permutation size, and new_dp computes counts for the next size.
Edge cases: If k exceeds the maximum possible inverse pairs, the final conditional returns zero. dp starts with one way to arrange zero elements with zero inversions.
Complexity: The number of processed states is O(min(k,n²)) overall, commonly bounded by O(nk), and space is O(k). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Select the maximum number of courses that can be completed before their deadlines, with each course requiring a duration.
Idea: Sort courses by deadline and keep selected durations in a max-heap, removing the longest duration whenever the total exceeds a deadline.
Technique and why it applies: Considering courses by earliest deadline preserves feasible prefixes. If the schedule is too long, dropping the longest course frees the most time while keeping the largest possible number of short courses.
Invariant: now is the total duration of courses currently retained in max_heap, and all retained courses processed so far meet their deadline after adjustment.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero. Negative durations are not expected; the heap stores negated durations to simulate a max-heap.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n) and each course causes heap operations O(log n), giving O(n log n) time and O(n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the smallest range containing at least one value from each of k sorted lists.
Idea: Initialize a min-heap with each list's first value and track the maximum value among the current selected elements.
Technique and why it applies: The heap minimum is the left endpoint of the current range and right is the maximum selected value. After considering the range, advance the list that supplied the minimum; the range is updated if narrower.
Invariant: The heap contains one current value from each list, and right is the largest of those values.
Edge cases: The algorithm assumes every list is nonempty. When the list containing the minimum is exhausted, no later range can include a value from that list, so it returns the best range found.
Complexity: Each list element enters and leaves the heap once, giving O(N log k) time and O(k) heap space for N total elements. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether nonnegative integer c can be expressed as a²+b² for integers a and b.
Idea: Increment a from zero to floor(sqrt(c)) and test whether the remaining value has an integer square root.
Technique and why it applies: For each a, the required b² is c-a². If sqrt of that remainder is integral, the pair is a witness.
Invariant: Every possible nonnegative a up to sqrt(c) is considered, and no larger a can satisfy a²≤c.
Edge cases: c=0 returns True immediately because sqrt(0) is integral. Floating-point square roots can be imprecise for large values, although the usual constraints are modest.
Complexity: The loop takes O(sqrt(c)) time and O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Check whether c is the sum of two integer squares.
Idea: Try each a up to the square root and compute the integer square root of c-a².
Technique and why it applies: For each a, b is set to floor(sqrt(c-a²)); equality a²+b²=c confirms that the remainder is a perfect square.
Invariant: Each loop iteration checks one candidate a, and all smaller candidates have already failed.
Edge cases: c=0 returns True using a=0 and b=0. The loop includes the exact square-root endpoint by adding one to the range bound.
Complexity: It performs O(sqrt(c)) iterations and O(1) extra space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Compute exclusive execution time for each function from nested start/end logs with inclusive end timestamps.
Idea: Use a call stack storing the active function and its latest unaccounted timestamp.
Technique and why it applies: On a nested start, elapsed time since the active function's timestamp is charged to that caller. On end, the current function receives timestamp-start+1, and the caller resumes at timestamp+1.
Invariant: The top stack entry identifies the active function, and its timestamp marks the first unit not yet charged to it.
Edge cases: End timestamps are inclusive, hence the +1. The log stream is assumed valid and properly nested.
Complexity: Each log is processed once, giving O(L) time for L logs; the stack uses O(depth) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return each function's exclusive runtime from nested start/end logs.
Idea: Track active function IDs in a stack and a global prev timestamp marking the next unaccounted time unit.
Technique and why it applies: When a function starts, the previous active function receives the elapsed interval before the new start. When a function ends, it receives an inclusive duration and prev advances one unit past the end timestamp.
Invariant: prev is the next timestamp to charge, and stk represents nested active calls.
Edge cases: Inclusive end times require adding one when a function ends. Valid logs ensure an end always has a matching active stack entry.
Complexity: The scan is O(L) time and O(depth) stack space. The author space label O(n) is a safe upper bound in terms of log count.

Task and constraints: Minimize the cost of purchasing the requested item quantities using individual prices or special bundle offers.
Idea: Recursively try each applicable offer and compare its cost with buying all remaining items individually, memoizing by needs tuple.
Technique and why it applies: An offer is usable only when it does not make any need negative and its price is cheaper than buying those items separately. The recursive state subtracts the offer quantities and adds its price.
Invariant: memo[needs] stores the minimum cost for exactly the remaining quantities.
Edge cases: The memo dictionary is a mutable default argument shared across calls, potentially leaking results between separate invocations. Offers with no useful quantity reduction can also cause recursion loops if allowed.
Complexity: The number of needs states is the product of (need_i+1), with each state checking all offers; time and memo space are exponential in item types/needs. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum shopping cost for needs using individual prices and special bundles.
Idea: Recursively process offers by index, either skipping an offer or applying it repeatedly while it remains feasible.
Technique and why it applies: The baseline branch moves to the next offer without using the current one. The apply branch subtracts quantities, recurses at the same offer index to allow reuse, and restores needs afterward.
Invariant: The helper returns the minimum cost using offers from index i onward for the current needs vector.
Edge cases: Needs are mutated during recursion but restored before returning. Offers that subtract nothing could recurse indefinitely, though valid offers normally contain at least one item and reduce needs.
Complexity: The state space is exponential in needs and offer combinations; memoization is absent, so repeated subproblems can cause a large runtime. Recursion depth depends on how many offers can be applied. The author labels O(n·2^n) are not a reliable bound for general input.

Task and constraints: Count decoding ways for a string containing digits and '*' wildcards, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Build a map of single-character and two-character decoding multiplicities, then use DP over prefixes.
Technique and why it applies: Each position contributes single-character decodings times the prior count plus valid two-character combinations times the count two positions back. The map stores wildcard multiplicities such as '*' and '**'.
Invariant: dp[i] is intended to represent the number of decodings for the prefix ending at the corresponding position.
Edge cases: The code accesses s[0], so empty input fails. It initializes dp[0] and dp[-1] then iterates indices from one, but references dp[i-2] at i=1, which wraps to dp[-1] and may not represent the empty prefix correctly. A zero dp causes early return.
Complexity: The intended DP is O(n) time and O(n) space, but the index convention and initialization need correctness review. No labels were supplied.
